# Public Records Request — Connecticut Freedom of Information Act

## When to use this

Use this whenever the Kingdom wants to know what a Connecticut public agency
actually did, said, or holds. A records request costs a stamp, requires nobody's
permission, and depends on nothing being conceded about the Kingdom's status —
which is precisely why it works when nothing else the Kingdom sends is being
answered.

Send it early, in the ordinary course, before anything is in dispute. In a
land-use matter the internal emails, the staff memoranda, the notes of the site
inspection, and the file on what the town required of the other assemblies on the
same street are all obtainable before a complaint is filed and without anyone's
leave. They routinely decide whether a dispute is worth having. Requests sent
after a complaint is filed arrive into a hostile posture and get the treatment
that posture earns.

It also works as a backstop. Where two ordinary letters to an office have gone
unanswered, a request under the statute is routed to a records officer rather than
to whoever ignored the first two, and an office behaves differently once a docket
number exists.

Use `government-correspondence` instead where the Kingdom wants a decision, a
permit, or a meeting. This form is for records, and only for records.

For a federal agency the statute is different — 5 U.S.C. § 552, with a
twenty-business-day determination period and an administrative appeal window set
by each agency's own regulations. Adapt the body; do not cite the Connecticut
sections to a federal agency.

## Before you send

- [ ] **The body is a public agency** within Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-200(1) — a state
      or municipal office, department, board, commission, authority, or official,
      and any committee of one. A private contractor is not, though records it
      generated for the agency and that the agency holds usually are.
- [ ] **The request goes to the right custodian** — the agency's designated
      records officer, or the town clerk, or the official who has custody of the
      records. A request addressed to a department head who has nothing to do with
      records sits on a desk while the clock does not run.
- [ ] **The records are described so a clerk who knows nothing about the matter
      could find them.** Name the office, the subject, the individuals whose
      correspondence is wanted, the document types, and the file or application
      number. Vagueness is the most common ground on which a request is lawfully
      refused.
- [ ] **The date range has both ends.** An open-ended range invites a refusal for
      burden and gives the agency a reason to negotiate rather than produce.
- [ ] **Native electronic format is requested** where the records are electronic.
      It preserves metadata, is searchable, and costs the agency less than
      copying, which removes the fee objection before it is made.
- [ ] **The fee waiver is asked for in this letter,** with one or two sentences of
      reason. Asked for in the original request it is often granted; asked for
      after a quote arrives it rarely is.
- [ ] **A ceiling on fees is stated** so that no charge is incurred without the
      Kingdom's authorisation.
- [ ] **The request asks for a written statement of the exemption claimed for
      every withholding and redaction,** and for production of the non-exempt
      portions of partly exempt records.
- [ ] **The date of transmission is fixed and provable.** The four-business-day
      period runs from the request, so keep the sent email, the certified mail
      receipt, or the clerk's date stamp.
- [ ] **A record is open in the Register of Public Records Requests,** carrying
      its FOI number, with the statutory response deadline computed and entered
      the day the request goes out.
- [ ] **The thirty-day appeal window is understood before sending,** and someone
      is responsible for watching it. It is jurisdictional and nothing revives it.

## The request

```
[APEX KINGDOM LETTERHEAD]

[DATE]

BY EMAIL TO [ADDRESS] AND BY CERTIFIED MAIL

[FULL NAME]
[Designated Records Officer / Town Clerk / TITLE]
[AGENCY, IN ITS FORMAL NAME]
[STREET ADDRESS]
[CITY], Connecticut [ZIP]

Re:  Request for public records under the Freedom of Information Act,
     Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-200 et seq.
     Subject: [ONE LINE — e.g., "Zoning application No. 2026-0000,
     000 Main Street"]
     Our reference: [FOI RECORD NUMBER]

Dear [MR./MS./MX.] [SURNAME]:

This is a request under the Connecticut Freedom of Information Act, Conn.
Gen. Stat. § 1-200 et seq., to inspect and copy the public records
described below. It is made by Apex Kingdom, a religious society and
charitable trust operating in [BRIDGEPORT].

1. RECORDS REQUESTED

   For the period [START DATE] to [END DATE], inclusive:

   (a) [DESCRIBE THE FIRST CATEGORY. NAME THE OFFICE, THE SUBJECT, AND THE
       DOCUMENT TYPE — e.g., "All correspondence, including email, between
       the Office of Planning and Zoning and any person concerning
       application No. 2026-0000."]

   (b) [SECOND CATEGORY — e.g., "All internal memoranda, staff reports,
       reviewer comments, and handwritten notes prepared in connection with
       application No. 2026-0000, including drafts."]

   (c) [THIRD CATEGORY, NAMING INDIVIDUALS WHERE KNOWN — e.g., "All email
       sent or received by [NAME], [TITLE], containing any of the terms
       [TERM], [TERM], or [TERM]."]

   (d) [WHERE A COMPARISON IS THE POINT, SAY SO PRECISELY — e.g., "For each
       application for a special permit for a place of assembly in the
       [ZONE] district decided between [DATE] and [DATE]: the application,
       the staff report, the minutes of the hearing, and the decision with
       its stated reasons."]

   (e) [ANY RETENTION SCHEDULE, INDEX, OR LOG THAT WOULD IDENTIFY FURTHER
       RESPONSIVE RECORDS — e.g., "The agency's records retention schedule
       for the categories above."]

   "Public records or files" is understood as defined in Conn. Gen. Stat.
   § 1-200(5), and this request extends to recorded data or information
   relating to the conduct of the public's business in whatever form it is
   kept, including email, text and instant messages, calendar entries,
   voicemail, and attachments, whether held on agency systems or on a
   personal device or account used for agency business.

2. FORMAT

   Please provide electronic records in their native electronic format,
   with metadata intact, delivered by email or on portable media. Where a
   record exists only on paper, please provide a scanned copy in PDF.
   Native production is ordinarily less costly to the agency than copying,
   and I ask that it be used for that reason as well.

   [WHERE VOLUME IS UNKNOWN: In the alternative, I am content to inspect
   the records in person at your offices at a mutually convenient time and
   to identify from that inspection the documents of which I need copies.]

3. FEES AND WAIVER

   I request a waiver or reduction of any fee under Conn. Gen. Stat.
   § 1-212(d). Apex Kingdom is a nonprofit religious and charitable body.
   These records are not sought for any commercial purpose or for personal
   benefit. They are sought in furtherance of the public interest, in that
   [ONE OR TWO SENTENCES — e.g., "they concern how the City applies its
   assembly-use standards to religious and non-religious applicants alike,
   a matter of general public concern in the neighbourhoods the Kingdom
   serves"].

   If a waiver is not granted, please tell me the estimated cost before any
   charge is incurred. I authorise fees up to [$25.00] without further
   approval and ask that you contact me before exceeding that amount, so
   that I may narrow the request if it would help.

4. PARTIAL PRODUCTION, WITHHOLDINGS, AND EXEMPTIONS

   If any responsive record is withheld in whole or in part, please:

   (a) produce all portions of the record that are not exempt, redacting
       only what is exempt;

   (b) identify each record or portion withheld, by date, author,
       recipient, and general subject; and

   (c) state in writing the specific subdivision of Conn. Gen. Stat.
       § 1-210(b), or other statute, relied on for each withholding.

   Please produce responsive records on a rolling basis as they are
   located, rather than holding all production until the last category is
   complete.

5. RESPONSE

   Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-206(a) requires that any denial of the right to
   inspect or copy be made in writing within four business days of this
   request, and provides that a failure to comply within that period is
   deemed a denial. If any part of this request is unclear, or if narrowing
   it would allow a faster or fuller response, please telephone or email me
   and I will work with you; I would much prefer to adjust the request than
   to receive a refusal for want of specificity.

   Please direct the response, and any question about this request, to me
   at the address, telephone number, and email above. I will follow up by
   telephone if I have not heard from your office by [DATE FOUR BUSINESS
   DAYS OUT].

Thank you for your assistance, and for the work your office does.

Respectfully,

______________________________
[FULL NAME]
[OFFICE HELD], Apex Kingdom
[STREET ADDRESS] · [TELEPHONE] · [EMAIL]
```

## Notes

**Specificity is the whole game.** An agency may lawfully refuse a request it
cannot reasonably identify records from, and a request phrased as "all documents
relating to the Kingdom" is such a request. The cure is mechanical: name the
office, name the subject, name the people whose correspondence is wanted, name the
document types, give the file number, and bound the period at both ends. A request
drafted that way is hard to refuse and easy for a clerk to work, and clerks
produce faster for requests they can work.

The offer in paragraph 5 to narrow the request is not a courtesy. It is the single
most effective line in the letter. It converts the records officer from a
gatekeeper into a collaborator, and it forecloses the refusal-for-vagueness that
would otherwise cost a month.

**Fees.** Under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-212 the per-page charge for copies is capped
by statute — a lower cap for state offices than for other public agencies — and
§ 1-211 governs records kept in a computer storage system, which the agency must
provide in printed form or on electronic medium. Section 1-212(d) requires a
waiver in defined circumstances, including where the agency determines the records
are sought in furtherance of the public interest and not for a commercial purpose.
Note the structure: the waiver is mandatory once the determination is made, but
the determination belongs to the agency. That is why the request supplies the
agency with the sentence it needs in order to make it. Ask in the original letter,
give the reason, and keep the reason honest and specific to these records.

**The four business days, and what they mean.** Section 1-206(a) requires a denial
to be in writing within four business days, and a failure to comply within that
period is deemed a denial. The statute allows a longer period where the request is
determined to be one for a large volume of records, so a substantial request may
properly draw a slower answer — but the agency has to say so. What it may not do
is simply go quiet. Silence past the fourth business day is a denial by operation
of law, and it starts the appeal clock whether anyone noticed or not. Compute the
date the day the request goes out, count business days rather than calendar days,
and exclude state holidays.

**The thirty-day appeal, which is where the leverage actually is.** From a
denial — actual or deemed — Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-206(b)(1) allows thirty days to
file a notice of appeal with the Freedom of Information Commission. The window is
jurisdictional. Nothing revives it: not a promise to look again, not a partial
production that arrives late, not an apology from the agency.

Filing costs nothing, requires no lawyer, and is done by a short written notice
identifying the requester, the agency, the records requested, the date of the
request, and the denial or the date the response period expired, with copies of
the correspondence attached. The Commission takes evidence, holds hearings, and
orders disclosure, and under § 1-206(b)(2) it may impose a civil penalty against
an official who denied access without reasonable grounds. Verify the Commission's
current filing address and any electronic filing option before sending; it sits in
Hartford and publishes both.

The practical effect is worth stating plainly, because it is the reason to use
this instrument at all. A great many appeals never reach a hearing. The agency
produces the records once a docket number exists, because defending a denial costs
staff time that producing the records does not. Record that outcome as the win it
is.

**Expect two lawful sources of delay, and do not read either as bad faith.**
Section 1-210(b) contains the exemptions — preliminary drafts and notes,
personnel and medical files whose disclosure would constitute an invasion of
personal privacy, records of law enforcement not otherwise available, attorney
work product, and others. And where personnel or medical files are requested,
§ 1-214 requires the agency to notify the employee, who has a short period in
which to object, after which the agency must decide. That procedure takes longer
than four days and is required by statute. What is not lawful is a withholding
with no exemption named, which is why paragraph 4 asks for the citation. An agency
that withholds without specifying the exemption has not made a lawful denial, and
saying so in one courteous sentence frequently produces the records without an
appeal.

**Requests inbound to the Kingdom.** A private religious association is not a
public agency within Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-200(1) and is generally under no
obligation to answer a request made under the Act. Say so once, courteously, and
stop — but understand that declining is a choice with consequences rather than a
default. Where the request concerns something the Kingdom is content to have
known, a considered voluntary response is usually better strategy than silence and
costs nothing. Where it concerns membership rolls, discipline files, donor
identities, or the personal data of minors, do not produce, refer it to Counsel,
and record the refusal and its reasons in the register. Silence and a reasoned
declination look very different when quoted back later.

**What this request is not.** It is a citizen's request under an ordinary statute,
made by a private body with no more authority than any resident of Bridgeport has.
It is not process, it commands nothing, and it asserts nothing about the Kingdom's
status. Nothing in it should be styled as an order, and no consequence should be
described as following automatically from the agency's silence except the one the
statute itself supplies.

---

*This is an operating template prepared to organise the Kingdom's affairs. It is
not legal advice and no attorney-client relationship arises from it. Statutory fee
caps, filing addresses, and agency procedures change, and the thirty-day appeal
window cannot be reopened once missed. Engage licensed Connecticut counsel before
acting on any of it.*
